claim: Plasmodium vivax is the most globally widespread of the six species of Plasmodium that cause malaria in humans.
source: Of the six species of Plasmodium that cause malaria in humans (Ansari et al., 2016), Plasmodium vivax is the most globally widespread (Howes et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ansari et al., 2016 and Howes et al., 2016

claim: Vivax malaria now accounts for the most malaria episodes in countries with successful falciparum malaria control programs.
source: Vivax malaria now accounts for the most malaria episodes in countries with successful falciparum malaria control programs (Price et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Price et al., 2020

claim: P. vivax sporozoites can invade hepatocytes and become quiescent hypnozoites.
source: Controlling vivax malaria is complicated by the ability of P. vivax sporozoites, the infectious stage inoculated by mosquitoes, to invade hepatocytes and become quiescent (Wells et al., 2010; White et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wells et al., 2010 and White et al., 2014

claim: Quiescent hypnozoites persist undetectable for months or even years before resuming growth and initiating a relapse blood stage infection.
source: These quiescent 'hypnozoites' persist, undetectable, for months or even years before resuming growth and initiating a 'relapse' blood stage infection, leading to subsequent transmission back to mosquitoes (Adams and Mueller, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Adams and Mueller, 2017

claim: P. vivax liver merozoites can immediately form gametocytes instead of first establishing an asexual stage blood infection.
source: New evidence suggests this transmission is expedited and silent as P. vivax liver merozoites can immediately form gametocytes instead of first having to establish an asexual stage blood infection, such as is the case for P. falciparum (Roth et al., 2018; Adapa et al., 2019; Schäfer et al., 2020; Mancio-Silva et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Roth et al., 2018; Adapa et al., 2019; Schäfer et al., 2020; Mancio-Silva et al., 2022

claim: A compound with radical cure efficacy removes all parasites from the patient, including hypnozoites in the liver.
source: Clinically, a compound with radical cure efficacy is one that removes all parasites from the patient, including hypnozoites in the liver (Campo et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Campo et al., 2015

claim: Hypnozoites are refractory to all antimalarials except the 8-aminoquinolines.
source: Hypnozoites are refractory to all antimalarials except the 8-aminoquinolines, which were first identified over 70 years ago using low-throughput screening in avian malaria models (Rangel and Llinás, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rangel and Llinás, 2021

claim: Primaquine efficacy is contingent on a large total dose administered in a 7- to 14-day regimen, leading to adherence problems.
source: Primaquine was the first 8-aminoquinoline widely used for radical cure; however, efficacy is contingent on a large total dose administered in a 7- to 14-day regimen, leading to adherence problems and infrequent use in malaria control programs of endemic countries (Taylor et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Taylor et al., 2019

claim: Tafenoquine lacks efficacy when co-administered with dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine.
source: Tafenoquine–chloroquine was developed from primaquine as an improved single dose for radical cure (Llanos-Cuentas et al., 2019), but a recent clinical trial shows tafenoquine lacks efficacy when co-administered with the common antimalarial dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine, calling into question tafenoquine's suitability in areas of high chloroquine resistance (Sutanto et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to Llanos-Cuentas et al., 2019 and Sutanto et al., 2023

claim: 8-aminoquinolines cannot be administered to pregnant women or glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase-deficient individuals.
source: Furthermore, 8-aminoquinolines cannot be administered to pregnant women or glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase-deficient individuals and are ineffective in persons with specific cytochrome P450 genotypes (Baird, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Baird, 2019

claim: The discovery and development of new chemical classes with radical cure activity are needed.
source: For these reasons, the discovery and development of new chemical classes with radical cure activity are needed (Burrows et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Burrows et al., 2017

claim: Modern drug discovery typically relies on phenotypic screening and protein target identification.
source: Modern drug discovery typically relies on phenotypic screening and protein target identification (Schenone et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schenone et al., 2013

claim: Current high-throughput screening for new antimalarials focuses almost entirely on blood or liver schizonts.
source: However, due to lower cost and higher feasibility, current high-throughput screening for new antimalarials focuses almost entirely on blood or liver schizonts (Avery et al., 2014; Antonova-Koch et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Avery et al., 2014 and Antonova-Koch et al., 2018

claim: High-throughput antimalarial screening with a target chemo-profile for killing hypnozoites has only recently been made possible.
source: High-throughput antimalarial screening with a target chemo-profile for killing hypnozoites has only recently been made possible with the introduction of cell-based phenotypic screening platforms featuring a monolayer of hepatocytes infected with sporozoites, a portion of which go on to form hypnozoites (Valenciano et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Valenciano et al., 2022

claim: The first hypnozonticidal hits from these platforms are just now being reported.
source: While the first hypnozonticidal hits from these platforms are just now being reported (Maher et al., 2021), protein target identification approaches for hypnozonticidal drug discovery are in their infancy as the transcriptome of hypnozoites has only recently been reported and robust methods for genetic manipulation of P. vivax are still underdeveloped (Ruberto et al., 2022; Bermúdez et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Maher et al., 2021, Ruberto et al., 2022, and Bermúdez et al., 2018

claim: The ReFRAME library consists of approximately 12,000 developmental, approved, and discontinued drugs.
source: This library consists of approximately 12,000 developmental, approved, and discontinued drugs with the expectation that the repurposing of compounds with some optimization or regulatory success could expedite the decade-long path drugs typically progress through from discovery to licensure (Janes et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Janes et al., 2018

claim: Hydralazine and cadralazine were found effective at killing hypnozoites.
source: Interestingly, two structurally related compounds used for treating hypertension, hydralazine and cadralazine, were found effective at killing hypnozoites.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the ReFRAME screen

claim: Hydralazine and cadralazine have been shown to modulate DNA methylation.
source: Because these inhibitors have been shown to modulate DNA methylation (Cornacchia et al., 1988; Singh et al., 2009), we pursued and confirmed the existence of methyl-cytosine modifications in P. vivax sporozoite and liver stages.
evidence: Supported by citations to Cornacchia et al., 1988 and Singh et al., 2009

claim: Hypnozoites were found to be susceptible to several classes of epigenetic inhibitors, including six distinct histone deacetylase inhibitors and two inhibitors targeting histone methylation.
source: Hypnozoites were found to be susceptible to several classes of epigenetic inhibitors, including six distinct histone deacetylase inhibitors and two inhibitors targeting histone methylation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the epigenetic inhibitor library screen

claim: MMV019721 selectively kills P. vivax and P. cynomolgi hypnozoites.
source: We found MMV019721 selectively kills P. vivax and P. cynomolgi hypnozoites, implicating acetyl-CoA synthetase as an additional hypnozonticidal drug target.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from dose-response assays

claim: Hypnozoites become insensitive to most legacy antimalarials after 5 days in culture.
source: Chemical biology approaches have shown that hypnozoites become insensitive to most legacy antimalarials after 5 days in culture, indicating they must mature following hepatocyte infection (Maher et al., 2021; Posfai et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Maher et al., 2021 and Posfai et al., 2020

claim: Hypnozoite maturation was noted in recent single-cell transcriptomic analyses of P. vivax liver stages.
source: Hypnozoite maturation was also noted in recent single-cell transcriptomic analyses of P. vivax liver stages, which demonstrate distinct population clusters of maturing and quiescent hypnozoites (Mancio-Silva et al., 2022; Ruberto et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mancio-Silva et al., 2022 and Ruberto et al., 2022

claim: Discovery and development of hit compounds with radical cure activity in vivo requires screening against mature hypnozoites in vitro.
source: Importantly, discovery and development of hit compounds with radical cure activity in vivo, which includes elimination of hypnozoites in the liver of malaria patients (Campo et al., 2015), requires screening against mature hypnozoites in vitro (Zeeman et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Campo et al., 2015 and Zeeman et al., 2016

claim: 36 P. vivax cases from either SMRU or IPC were needed to complete the primary screen over the course of 18 months.
source: The screening library was divided between both sites to enable concurrent progress; ultimately, 36 P. vivax cases from either site were needed to complete the primary screen over the course of 18 months (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the primary screen

claim: 72 compounds were selected for confirmation of activity against hypnozoites in a dose–response format.
source: We selected 72 compounds for confirmation of activity against hypnozoites in a dose–response format.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the confirmation assays

claim: Following confirmation in dose–response assays, some hits exhibited moderate selectivity and potency, with pEC50's ranging from 5.42 to 7.07.
source: Following confirmation in dose–response assays, some hits exhibited moderate selectivity and potency, with pEC50's ranging from 5.42 to 7.07 (pEC50 is the inverse log of potency in M concentration, e.g. pEC50 3 = 1 mM, pEC50 6 = 1 μM, and pEC50 9 = 1 nM) (Table 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from dose-response assays

claim: Poziotinib inhibits HER2, a tyrosine protein kinase associated with the downregulation of apoptosis and metastasis.
source: As an example, poziotinib inhibits HER2, a tyrosine protein kinase associated with the downregulation of apoptosis and metastasis (Kavarthapu et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kavarthapu et al., 2021

claim: Host apoptotic pathways are downregulated in P. vivax-infected hepatocytes.
source: We recently reported that host apoptotic pathways are downregulated in P. vivax-infected hepatocytes (Ruberto et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ruberto et al., 2022

claim: MS-0735 is an analog of MMV018983, a ribonucleotide-reductase (RNR) inhibitor.
source: MS-0735, an analog of our previously reported hypnozonticidal hit, MMV018983 (Maher et al., 2021), is a ribonucleotide-reductase (RNR) inhibitor and used as an antiviral.
evidence: Supported by citation to Maher et al., 2021

claim: RNR is critical for DNA damage repair.
source: However, it has been reported that RNR is also critical for DNA damage repair (Elledge et al., 1992), is important for maintaining cancer cell dormancy (Evans and Lin, 2015), and is expressed in P. vivax liver schizonts and hypnozoites (Ruberto et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Elledge et al., 1992, Evans and Lin, 2015, and Ruberto et al., 2022

claim: Narasin and plasmocid were rediscovered as previously reported hypnozonticidal compounds.
source: We also rediscovered previously reported hypnozonticidal compounds included in the library, including the ionophore narasin (Maher et al., 2021) and the 8-aminoquinoline plasmocid (Schmidt and Schmidt, 1949; Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Table 1).
evidence: Supported by citations to Maher et al., 2021 and Schmidt and Schmidt, 1949

claim: Three hydrazinophthalazines analogs – cadralazine, pildralazine, and hydralazine – were active against mature hypnozoites.
source: Three hydrazinophthalazines analogs – cadralazine, pildralazine, and hydralazine – were active against mature hypnozoites, with cadralazine displaying the best combination of potency (pEC50 = 6.33 ± 0.33), maximal inhibition near 100%, and selectivity over PHH (>21-fold), HEK293T (>85-fold), and HepG2 (>79-fold) cells (Figure 1B, Table 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from dose-response assays

claim: Hydralazine was FDA-approved in 1953 and is currently one of the world's most-prescribed antihypertensives.
source: Hydralazine, which was FDA-approved in 1953, is currently one of the world's most-prescribed antihypertensives, and on the WHO list of essential medicines (World Health Organization, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to World Health Organization, 2019

claim: Cadralazine was developed in the 1980s as an improvement over hydralazine but was abandoned due to side effects.
source: Cadralazine, which was developed in the 1980s as an improvement over hydralazine, was abandoned due to side effects and only licensed in Italy and Japan (McTavish et al., 1990).
evidence: Supported by citation to McTavish et al., 1990

claim: Hydrazinophthalazines have been shown to inhibit human DNA methyltransferases (DNMT).
source: Hydrazinophthalazines have been shown to inhibit human DNA methyltransferases (DNMT) (Cornacchia et al., 1988; Singh et al., 2009) and hydralazine has also been recently used to study potential DNA methylation patterns in the P. falciparum asexual blood stages (Ponts et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cornacchia et al., 1988, Singh et al., 2009, and Ponts et al., 2013

claim: Hydrazinophthalazines were inactive when tested against P. berghei liver schizonts, P. cynomolgi asexual blood stages, and P. falciparum asexual blood stages.
source: Similar to our previous report (Ponts et al., 2013), these hydrazinophthalazines were inactive when tested against P. berghei liver schizonts, P. cynomolgi asexual blood stages, and P. falciparum asexual blood stages (Table 1—source data 1), suggesting that hypnozoite quiescence may be biologically distinct from developing schizonts (Maher et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from counterscreen assays and citation to Ponts et al., 2013 and Maher et al., 2021

claim: Hydralazine and cadralazine were not identified as potential hits in any of the 112 bioassay screens of the ReFRAME published to date.
source: Hydralazine and cadralazine were not identified as potential hits in any of the 112 bioassay screens of the ReFRAME published to date (Su, 2024), suggesting these compounds specifically target P. vivax liver stages and not promiscuously active compounds.
evidence: Supported by citation to Su, 2024

claim: The hypnozonticidal activity and potency of cadralazine, hydralazine, and poziotinib were independently confirmed at NITD.
source: Select hits were shared with the Novartis Institute for Tropical Diseases (NITD), where the hypnozonticidal activity and potency of cadralazine (pEC50 = 6.09 ± 0.45), hydralazine (pEC50 = 6.20), and poziotinib (pEC50 = 6.17) were independently confirmed in a similar 8-day P. vivax screening platform using a P. vivax case from southern Thailand (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from independent confirmation assays

claim: The 30 mg/kg dose of cadralazine resulted in maximum plasma concentration of 13.7 μg/ml (or 48.2 μM) and half-life of 2.19 ± 0.24 hr in rhesus macaques.
source: The 30 mg/kg dose resulted in maximum plasma concentration of 13.7 μg/ml (or 48.2 μM) and half-life of 2.19 ± 0.24 hr, which was sufficient to cover the in vitro EC90 for several hours without noticeable side effects (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from pharmacokinetic study

claim: Hydralazine and cadralazine were found inactive against P. cynomolgi hypnozoites when tested in all three different PSH donor lots.
source: While poziotinib was active against P. cynomolgi hypnozoites when tested in two of three different PSH donor lots (pEC50 = 5.67 and 5.95) (Supplementary file 2) hydralazine and cadralazine were found inactive when tested in all three different PSH donor lots (Figure 1B, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from P. cynomolgi assays

claim: When tested alone in dose–response from 50 μM, 5-azacytidine had no effect on hypnozoites.
source: When tested alone in dose–response from 50 μM, 5-azacytidine had no effect on hypnozoites.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from drug combination studies

claim: When added to cadralazine in fixed ratio combinations, 5-azacytidine increased the potency of cadralazine by ~2-fold across several combinations.
source: However, when added to cadralazine in fixed ratio combinations ranging from 8:1 to 1:8, 5-azacytidine increased the potency of cadralazine by ~2-fold across several combinations in two independent experiments (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from drug combination studies

claim: The most potent effect was detected using a 2:1 fixed ratio of cadralazine:5-azacytidine, resulting in an equivalent EC50 decrease from 470 to 216 nM.
source: The most potent effect was detected using a 2:1 fixed ratio of cadralazine:5-azacytidine, resulting in an equivalent EC50 decrease from 470 to 216 nM.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from drug combination studies

claim: Clear evidence of 5mC, but not 5hmC, was found in both P. vivax schizonts and hypnozoites.
source: We found clear evidence of 5mC, but not 5hmC, in both schizonts and hypnozoites, morphologically consistent with the presence of 5mC in the parasite's nucleus (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from immunofluorescence staining

claim: The net 5hmC area per parasite was found significantly lower when compared to 5mC signals.
source: While some evidence of 5hmC-positive forms did appear from this analysis, the net 5hmC area per parasite was found significantly lower when compared to 5mC signals (Kruskal–Wallis tests, for hypnozoites H(7) = 194.3, p < 0.0001, for schizonts H(7) = 88.66, p < 0.0001).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from high-content quantification

claim: Similar results on the ratio of 5hmC to 5mC were also recently reported in P. falciparum blood stages.
source: Similar results on the ratio of 5hmC to 5mC were also recently reported in P. falciparum blood stages (Lenz et al., 2024), confirming that 5mC marks are the predominant DNA methylation marks in both species.
evidence: Supported by citation to Lenz et al., 2024

claim: Both P. cynomolgi liver schizonts and hypnozoites are positive for 5mC, but not 5hmC.
source: Like P. vivax, we found both P. cynomolgi liver schizonts and hypnozoites are positive for 5mC, but not 5hmC.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from immunofluorescence staining

claim: The 5mC stain morphology and intensity were relatively lower in P. cynomolgi hypnozoites versus P. vivax hypnozoites.
source: However, the 5mC stain morphology and intensity were relatively lower in P. cynomolgi hypnozoites versus P. vivax hypnozoites, suggesting potential divergence of DNA methylation pathways in these two species (Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from immunofluorescence staining

claim: The average 5mC level detected across all cytosines was 0.49% and 0.39% for P. vivax and P. cynomolgi, respectively.
source: The average 5mC level detected across all cytosines was 0.49% and 0.39% for P. vivax and P. cynomolgi, respectively.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from bisulfite sequencing

claim: These percentages are comparable to the 0.58% methylation level detected in P. falciparum blood stages.
source: These percentages are comparable to the 0.58% methylation level detected in P. falciparum blood stages (Ponts et al., 2013), but likely underestimate methylated loci considering the coverage we achieved (see methods).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ponts et al., 2013

claim: A stable methylation level was observed throughout the genomes, including in telomeric and sub-telomeric regions.
source: We then monitored the distribution of detected 5mC along the P. vivax and P. cynomolgi chromosomes (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplements 2 and 3) and observed a stable methylation level throughout the genomes, including in telomeric and sub-telomeric regions.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from bisulfite sequencing

claim: Methylation was detected as asymmetrical, with CHH at 69.5% and 70.5%, CG at 16% and 15.7%, and CHG at 14.3% and 13.64%, for P. vivax and P. cynomolgi, respectively.
source: We further examined the context of genome-wide methylations and, similar to what we previously observed in P. falciparum (Ponts et al., 2013), methylation was detected as asymmetrical, with CHH (where H can be any nucleotide but G) at 69.5% and 70.5%, CG at 16% and 15.7%, and CHG at 14.3% and 13.64%, for P. vivax and P. cynomolgi, respectively (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from bisulfite sequencing and citation to Ponts et al., 2013

claim: A slightly increased distribution of 5mC was observed in promoters and exons compared to the intronic region, as well as in the template versus non-template strand, in P. vivax and P. cynomolgi.
source: We observed a slightly increased distribution of 5mC in promoters and exons compared to the intronic region, as well as in the template versus non-template strand, in P. vivax and P. cynomolgi.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from bisulfite sequencing

claim: These results were consistent with previous data obtained in P. falciparum and in plants.
source: These results were consistent with previous data obtained in P. falciparum and in plants (Ponts et al., 2013; Lucky et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ponts et al., 2013 and Lucky et al., 2023

claim: An inverse relationship was revealed between methylation and mRNA abundance in the proximal promoter regions and the beginning of the gene bodies, with highly expressed genes appearing hypomethylated and weakly expressed genes hypermethylated.
source: The 5mC levels in 5′ flanking regions, gene bodies, and 3′ flanking regions were placed into five bins and compared to mRNA abundance, revealing an inverse relationship between methylation and mRNA abundance in the proximal promoter regions and the beginning of the gene bodies, with highly expressed genes appearing hypomethylated and weakly expressed genes hypermethylated (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from bisulfite sequencing and transcriptomic data

claim: Methylation level in proximal promoter regions as well as in the first exon of the genes may affect, at least partially, gene expression in malaria parasites.
source: These results suggest that methylation level in proximal promoter regions as well as in the first exon of the genes may affect, at least partially, gene expression in malaria parasites.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data from bisulfite sequencing and transcriptomic data

claim: 5mC is present at a low level in P. vivax and P. cynomolgi sporozoites and could control liver stage development and hypnozoite quiescence.
source: While these data will need to be further validated and linked to hypnozoite formation at a single-cell level, we have determined that 5mC is present at a low level in P. vivax and P. cynomolgi sporozoites and could control liver stage development and hypnozoite quiescence.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from bisulfite sequencing and speculation about function

claim: 100 μM of 1-ABT was sufficient to completely reduce CYP3A4 activity in both basal and rifampicin-induced PHH.
source: We used a cytochrome P450 functional assay specific to CYP3A4 and determined that 100 μM of 1-ABT was sufficient to completely reduce CYP3A4 activity in both basal and rifampicin-induced PHH (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from CYP3A4 functional assay

claim: Treatment with 100 μM 1-ABT resulted in a 75% decrease in CYP3A4 activity, a more than 60% reduction of CYP2B6 and CYP2E1 activity, and lesser effects on CYP2C9, CYP1A2, and CYP2D6.
source: This effect was further confirmed and quantified by mass spectrometry after 1 hr of treatment at 100 μM 1-ABT. We not only detected a 75% decrease in CYP3A4 activity, but also a more than 60% reduction of CYP2B6 and CYP2E1 activity along with lesser effects on CYP2C9, CYP1A2, and CYP2D6 (Figure 5).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from mass spectrometry

claim: The modified assay did not drastically affect the potency of most hits.
source: The modified assay did not drastically affect the potency of most hits (Figure 5—figure supplement 3), but helped resolve the hypnozonticidal activity of poziotinib (pEC50 = 6.05), which had been previously confirmed in P. vivax and P. cynomolgi assays performed at NITD (Figure 5—figure supplement 2, Supplementary file 2, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from validation assays

claim: Eleven compounds targeting five different epigenetic mechanisms were confirmed to have selective hypnozonticidal potency.
source: We confirmed our initial hits in dose–response assays resulting in selective hypnozonticidal potency for 11 compounds targeting five different epigenetic mechanisms (Table 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from dose-response assays

claim: Histone deacetylase inhibitors with hypnozonticidal activity include panobinostat (pEC50 = 6.98 ± 0.18), AR42 (pEC50 = 6.11 ± 0.24), abexinostat (pEC50 = 5.48 ± 0.00), givinostat (pEC50 = 5.35 ± 0.45), practinostat (pEC50 = 5.32 ± 0.13), and raddeanin A (pEC50 = 5.95 ± 0.00).
source: This includes the histone deacetylase inhibitors panobinostat (pEC50 = 6.98 ± 0.18), AR42 (pEC50 = 6.11 ± 0.24), abexinostat (pEC50 = 5.48 ± 0.00), givinostat (pEC50 = 5.35 ± 0.45), practinostat (pEC50 = 5.32 ± 0.13), and raddeanin A (pEC50 = 5.95 ± 0.00).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from dose-response assays

claim: Histone methyltransferase inhibitor hits included MI2 (pEC50 = 5.48 ± 0.00) and cyproheptadine (pEC50 = 5.24 ± 0.34).
source: Histone methyltransferase inhibitor hits included MI2 (pEC50 = 5.48 ± 0.00), a compound that targets the interaction between menin (a global regulator of gene expression), and MLL (a DNA-binding protein that methylates histone H3 lysine 4 Cierpicki and Grembecka, 2014), and cyproheptadine (pEC50 = 5.24 ± 0.34), which targets the SET-domain-containing lysine methyltransferase (Hirano et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from dose-response assays and citations to Cierpicki and Grembecka, 2014 and Hirano et al., 2018

claim: MMV019721 was found to be selectively active on mature P. vivax hypnozoites.
source: We found that one compound, MMV019721, was selectively active on mature P. vivax hypnozoites (Table 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from dose-response assays

claim: MMV019721 is directly targeting P. falciparum ACS.
source: Given the evidence, MMV019721 is directly targeting P. falciparum ACS (Summers et al., 2022), this result suggests ACS also is a hypnozonticidal drug target.
evidence: Supported by citation to Summers et al., 2022

claim: This work represents one of the first applications of a radical cure development pipeline to begin with in vitro screening against P. vivax hypnozoites and end with attempted confirmation using P. cynomolgi radical cure models.
source: As such, this work represents one of the first applications of a radical cure development pipeline to begin with in vitro screening against P. vivax hypnozoites and end with attempted confirmation using P. cynomolgi radical cure models.
evidence: Based on the overall experimental approach described in the manuscript

claim: There is sufficient diversity in gene expression, structural biology, or mechanisms of hepatic quiescence between P. cynomolgi and P. vivax hypnozoites that some newly identified hits may be species-specific.
source: While further studies will be needed to confirm that targets of our hits are parasite- or host-directed, our data show there is sufficient diversity in gene expression, structural biology, or mechanisms of hepatic quiescence between P. cynomolgi and P. vivax hypnozoites that some newly identified hits may be species-specific.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing differential activity of hits against P. vivax and P. cynomolgi

claim: The role of the rhesus macaque radical cure model in the radical cure drug development cascade may need to be reevaluated.
source: While this result could also be attributed to differential metabolism in human and monkey hepatocytes (Liang et al., 2020), the rhesus macaque radical cure model is currently considered an important prerequisite for continued drug development, including efficacy testing in controlled human infections. The role of this model in the radical cure drug development cascade may need to be reevaluated as some compounds identified as promising for the radical cure of P. vivax may be abandoned too quickly due to the lack of activity against P. cynomolgi.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data and citation to Liang et al., 2020

claim: Epigenetic control of pathogenic dormancy via DNA methylation is a pathway that could be potentially targeted by future antimalarials.
source: In addition to the identification of promising new hits and direction, our data suggests that epigenetic control of pathogenic dormancy via DNA methylation is a pathway that could be potentially targeted by future antimalarials.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing activity of DNA methylation inhibitors

claim: DNA methylation has been validated as controlling critical processes in plants, which share evolutionary traits with Plasmodium.
source: DNA methylation has also been validated as controlling critical processes in plants, which share evolutionary traits with Plasmodium (Merrick, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Merrick, 2021

claim: DNA methylation in the genus Plasmodium was first described in P. falciparum blood stages.
source: DNA methylation in the genus Plasmodium was first described in P. falciparum blood stages (Ponts et al., 2013) and has been associated with gene expression, transcriptional elongation, and parasite growth (Lucky et al., 2023; Hammam et al., 2021; Lenz et al., 2024).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ponts et al., 2013, Lucky et al., 2023, Hammam et al., 2021, and Lenz et al., 2024

claim: Hydralazine can directly inhibit DNA methylation in nuclear extracts of blood stage parasites and inhibit a recombinant functional fragment of the P. falciparum DNMT.
source: Previous experiments have shown that hydralazine can directly inhibit DNA methylation in nuclear extracts of blood stage parasites but also inhibit a recombinant functional fragment of the P. falciparum DNMT (Ponts et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ponts et al., 2013

claim: The current model of hypnozoite quiescence suggests RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) drive hypnozoite formation by preventing translation of target mRNAs associated with schizogony.
source: The current model of hypnozoite quiescence suggests RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) drive hypnozoite formation by preventing translation of target mRNAs associated with schizogony (Toenhake et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Toenhake et al., 2023

claim: In the current model, histone acetylation results in euchromatin at the loci of RBPs, resulting in their expression and ongoing quiescence.
source: In this model, histone acetylation results in euchromatin at the loci of RBPs, resulting in their expression and ongoing quiescence.
evidence: Based on the current model of hypnozoite quiescence

claim: It is likely that the identified RBPs are part of broader gene networks which, when perturbed by sudden modulation of epigenetic features such as DNA methylation and histone acetylation, result in a lethal level of dysregulation.

claim: The chemical probes described in this report could be used in combination with single-cell technology to more precisely perturb hypnozoites and refine our understanding of epigenetic pathways regulating hypnozoite formation and survival.
source: While we still need to develop P. vivax transgenic lines to successfully study hypnozoite biology and further validate potential drug targets (Voorberg-van der Wel et al., 2020; Wel et al., 2021), the chemical probes that we described in this report could be used in combination with single-cell technology to more precisely perturb hypnozoites and refine our understanding of epigenetic pathways regulating hypnozoite formation and survival.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of experimental data and citations to Voorberg-van der Wel et al., 2020 and Wel et al., 2021

claim: The ReFRAME library was screened using an 8-day radical cure assay in which developing liver schizonts and mature, PI4Ki-insensitive hypnozoites were treated on days 5–7 post-infection.
source: The ReFRAME library was screened using the original, 8-day radical cure assay, in which developing liver schizonts and mature, PI4Ki-insensitive hypnozoites were treated on days 5–7 post-infection (Roth et al., 2018; Maher et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Roth et al., 2018 and Maher et al., 2021

source: A total of 161 and 147 million high-quality reads were sequenced for P. vivax and P. cynomolgi samples, respectively (Supplementary file 3).
